commentary.bottom_line: Seven studies test citation verification, and all report that it catches or prevents fabricated and misattributed references, but six are automated benchmarks and one is an uncontrolled review of 20 synthetic cases. None measures whether verification during deployment reduces errors that reach clinicians or patients, or what it costs in reviewer time.

perspectives.view: Six of seven tests are level 5 automated benchmarks, and the seventh is a pre-post study without a comparator using 20 synthetic cases. The results point in one direction, but the evidence is indirect because it tests verification tools in offline settings rather than evaluators working in deployment. Samples are small or unrepresentative, so certainty is very low.

In one hazard study, 68.9% of ChatGPT neurosurgical references were inaccurate and 33.9% were falsified. Chain-of-Verification detected 60 of 62 problematic references (sensitivity 96.8%, specificity 98.6%). One agent verifier caught all injected attribution swaps, yet its source-plus-relation accuracy fell to 0.229 on a harder multi-source benchmark, which suggests detection may weaken as outputs grow complex.

Live PMID verification alone produced 0.0% fabricated and 0.0% wrong-topic citations, compared with 95.9% wrong-topic citations in unguided output. Adding programmatic citation checks moved one system from last (55.5) to first (81.8), which suggests evaluation design can change conclusions. In the one deployment test, 56 of 60 source-attributed statements were fully covered by the cited excerpt.

One Brazilian benchmark of 500 non-English clinical queries found 461 of 500 correct citations with deterministic verification versus 1 of 500 with prompt-based citation. A Turkish hazard study reported ChatGPT perfect-reference rates of 78.5% in Turkish and 71.4% in English, which suggests citation reliability may vary by language.

The NIST Generative AI Profile states that organizations should review and verify sources and citations during pre-deployment measurement and ongoing monitoring. This framework is voluntary guidance, and none of the supplied studies evaluates adherence to it or its effect on outcomes.

No study reports staff time, cost, or the effort needed to verify citations at scale. The tested methods were largely automated, including one that screened 8,050 references against expert adjudication, which suggests automation could reduce manual review, though no study measured workload directly.

In ratings and interviews involving oncology physicians, trust declined when citations did not match claims or provenance was buried. Two studies found chatbot answers scored 0 on JAMA source-attribution benchmarks, so patients reading such answers may have had no way to check where claims came from.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployed systems monitored with and without citation verification. Such a study would measure the rate of fabricated or misattributed citations reaching clinicians or patients, reviewer time per output, and the performance of manual versus automated checks on multi-source clinical answers. It would also report results separately for non-English and patient-facing use.
commentary.underserved_note: One test, a Brazilian benchmark, used non-English clinical queries, and no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving those groups have almost no evidence on whether verification performs as reported for their patients, particularly for patient-facing content in languages other than English.
